title: French Fry-Sized Fish Conquer a 50-Foot Waterfall!
summary: Imagine a fish climbing a wall of rushing water as tall as a five-story building. Sounds impossible, right? But in the Democratic Republic of Congo, tiny shellear fish do just that at Luvilombo Falls. These little swimmers are only about the size of a French fry—under two inches long—yet they scale a 50-foot (15-meter) vertical rock face. Scientists finally proved it after years of rumors. A researcher named P. Kiwele Mutambala led a team to the falls in 2018 and 2020. They watched in amazement as the fish inched upward against the powerful current. "It's as if the fish is swimming but in vertical," Mutambala said. "It's beyond imagination." How do they do it? The fish have microscopic hooks on their front fins that grip the slippery rock like Velcro. Their back fins push them forward. But it's not easy. They climb in short bursts, then rest for up to an hour. Many lose their grip and tumble back down, forcing them to start over. A single trip can take 10 hours! Only the smallest fish try this climb. Adults can grow up to four inches, but those over two inches seem too heavy. Scientists aren't sure why they do it. Maybe they're looking for food, safer homes, or mates. Whatever the reason, it's an incredible feat for such a tiny creature. This is the first climbing fish found in Africa, but not the only one in the world. In Hawaii, stream gobies use a suction cup on their bellies to climb waterfalls too. Nature is full of surprises!
why_it_matters: This tiny fish proves that even the smallest creatures can do things that seem impossible, teaching us that size doesn't limit what you can achieve.
